claims.text: At elevated temperatures in an oxidizing environment, a stable, adherent oxide scale is the primary factor governing the wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings.
The oxide scale reduces severe metal-to-metal contact and mitigates abrasive and adhesive wear.
The baseline is an approximately 5 μm FeNiCrCoCu coating on a conventional steel substrate.
The baseline coating has a uniform microstructure and minimal initial oxide content after controlled near-ambient deposition.
Increasing the coating temperature from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C under oxidizing conditions promotes surface oxide formation.
The proposed mechanism applies from ambient temperature to approximately 800 °C under moderate contact loads in dry or mildly humid air.
Heating produces a predominantly spinel and/or mixed-oxide film on the FeNiCrCoCu surface.
The growing oxide film limits direct contact between surface asperities.
The oxide film reduces metal-to-metal adhesion and plastic deformation.
The oxide film impedes crack propagation.
Higher-temperature oxide formation decreases overall wear loss and friction.
Elevated-temperature exposure will reduce wear rate by approximately 20–50% relative to room-temperature testing.
The coefficient of friction will decrease as the oxide film thickens and stabilizes.
At room temperature, the baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating exhibits moderate wear.
At room temperature, the baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating has limited oxide formation.
Outside the ambient-to-800 °C range, the protective oxide scale may not form effectively.
Under non-oxidizing atmospheres, the protective oxide-scale mechanism may not apply.
If wear does not improve with temperature in air, or if wear is unchanged between oxidizing and inert atmospheres, oxide-scale formation is not the primary governing mechanism.
